catalog_quote: In words of two syllables the accent is usually placed on the first syllable: as "male" ("rice") = "má-le"; "bende" ("dirt") = "bén-de"; "kubbe" ("ashes" or "dust") = "kúb-be"; "heri" ("peace") = "hé-ri." In words of three syllables, if they are simple words, the accent is on the antepenult: as "hárrige" ("lot" or "portion"); "yámmine" ("a kingdom"); "béllaχe" ("a hand"); "wéllaχe" ("a wooden slate"). In compound words the accent retains the place it has in the simple words.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: LOCATOR CHECK. Opened (136 pp., archive.org readingbookinsos00dougiala), ran extracted text on pp. 18-19 and rendered both pages to PNG and read the images. Printed pp. 6-7 of the Introduction, section headed "ACCENT", contain the quoted passage. It is verbatim except that the print marks the accented syllable with an acute in every example ("má-le", "bén-de", "kúb-be", "hé-ri", "hárrige", "yámmine", "béllaχe", "wéllaχe", with Greek chi for the kh sound), which the report's quote renders without accents and with x; the sentence about compound words follows immediately, as quoted. So the locator and wording are right. IDENTITY. Title page: "Rev. P. H. Douglin.. late S.P.G. West Indian missio…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the first syllable: on the initial syllable of disyllables ('usually') and on the antepenult, i.e. the first syllable, of simple trisyllables; compounds keep the accent of each simple member (so a compound has more than one accent).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; compounds retain the accent of each simple constituent.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'usually' for disyllables; only simple (non-compound) trisyllables are covered; no data on longer words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (reading pronunciation of isolated words in a teacher's introduction). Modern descriptions (Sangster & Faber 1968; Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013) treat Susu as a tone language with H/L melodies and say nothing about stress; Douglin's 'accent' is a 19th-century missionary's impression and may reflect the H-initial tonal melodies rather than a stress accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Douglin 1887 describes the Susu of the Rio Pongo (Guinea) / Sierra Leone SPG mission area ('Soso-land'); he notes only one dialect difference (Moria s > sh). Glottolog lists susu1250 without dialect subdivisions, so the statement is for the language as a whole; the 19th-century 'accent' should be read against the modern tonal analyses (Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013; Sangster & Faber 1968), which describe Susu as a two-tone language and are silent on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Green, Christopher R. & Maria Konoshenko. 2022. Tonal head marking in Mande compounds: endpoint neutralization and outliers. Mandenkan 67: 3-44. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.2699
tone_statements.quote: In Susu (2), the W2 is also morphologically lowered, but the final H tone of the W1’s melody spreads onto the first TBU of W2, as in (2a,b). In addition to the neutralization of the W2 melody, the lexical tones of W1 are also affected by rules of raising (HL#L → HH#L, 2c-d) or settling (LH#H → LL#H, 2b). Both rules are common across Mande; see Section 3 and discussion in Konoshenko (2014a). The rule of H spreading from W1 is likewise well-attested, though it is predominantly observed only in one branch of the family, as discussed below.
tone_statements.locator: Introduction, paragraph 5 (HTML edition), with examples (2a-d) in para 3; table (24) in para 120

tone_statements.citation: Green, Christopher R. 2018. A survey of word-level replacive tonal patterns in Western Mande. Mandenkan 59. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.1420
tone_statements.quote: Green, Anderson, & Obeng (2013) argue that the word‑level RT patterns in Susu are most similar to those observed in Mende. That is, the last tone of W1 is copied onto the first TBU of W2. These authors propose other downstream processes, namely affaissement and its counterpart raising, in order to account for other instances of neutralizations such as /LHH/ → [LLH] and /HLL/ → [HHL]. A series of nearly identical outcomes is reported for Yalunka in Keita (1989). Thus, from the standpoint of word‑level RT, languages of the Soso‑Jalonke are well placed alongside most other Southwestern Mande languages.
tone_statements.locator: section 'Soso-Jalonke (Susu-Yalunka)', paragraph 112 (HTML edition; examples in (29), para 111)
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (H, L) underlying, per the transcriptions and discussion
